questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Horizontal velocity in a projectile flight
questions.learningObjective: state why a projectile's horizontal speed does not change
questions.stem: A ball is thrown through the air with both a horizontal and an upward velocity, and it is later caught at the same height. Why is the horizontal velocity the same at the start and at the catch?

options.text: The ball's speed stays constant, so every component of it must stay constant
options.misconception: confuses an unchanged horizontal component with an unchanged total speed

options.text: The air is thin at the top of the arc, so the ball meets less resistance
options.misconception: invents a height-dependent air resistance that the question does not mention

options.text: The ball's mass is fixed, so no force can change how fast it moves sideways
options.misconception: confuses a fixed mass with a fixed velocity

options.text: Gravity acts only downwards, so it has no component to change the horizontal speed

questions.explanation: Once the ball is in the air the only force on it is its weight, which points straight down, so there is no force along the horizontal direction and the horizontal velocity cannot change. That is Newton's first law applied to one axis at a time. The total speed is not constant, because gravity does change the vertical component, and the mass of the ball has nothing to do with it: doubling the mass changes the accelerations the forces produce, not their absence. A projectile landing at its launch height ends with the same vertical component it started with but pointing down, and the same horizontal component throughout.
questions.hint: Ask which direction gravity acts in, and whether it has any part along the horizontal.

questions.topic: Resolving a launch velocity
questions.learningObjective: split a launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components
questions.stem: Resolving a 20 m/s launch at 60 degrees above the horizontal into two components does not change the speed. What is that speed in m/s once the components are known separately?
questions.explanation: Resolving the launch gives a horizontal component of 10 m/s and a vertical component of 17.3 m/s, and combining them as perpendicular vectors returns the root of their squares, which is 20 m/s, the original launch speed. Nothing has happened to the ball's speed at the instant of launch: the components are just a different way of stating the same velocity. The point of resolving is what comes next, since only the vertical component then changes under gravity while the horizontal one is untouched.
questions.hint: Split the launch into components, then rebuild the speed with Pythagoras.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Time of flight of a projectile
questions.learningObjective: find the time a projectile spends in the air
questions.stem: A ball leaves the hand at 20 m/s and 60 degrees above the horizontal, landing at its launch height. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, how long in seconds does it stay in the air?
questions.explanation: Only the vertical motion decides the flight time, and the vertical launch component is 20 x sin 60, which is 17.3 m/s. Setting the vertical displacement back to zero after the launch gives twice that component over g, so t = 2 x 17.3 over 9.8, which is 3.53 s. Stepping the vertical motion in small time slices returns the same figure, since the height returns to zero only when the upward and downward parts have taken the same time, and no horizontal reasoning can change that.
questions.hint: Only the vertical component matters, and the rise and fall take equal times.

questions.topic: Height gained on the way up

questions.stem: Rising from its launch point, a ball thrown at 20 m/s and 60 degrees reaches a highest point before returning to the launch height. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, what is that greatest height in m above the launch point?
questions.explanation: The height peaks when the vertical component has fallen to zero, so the square of that component over twice g gives the height, 17.3 squared over 19.6, which is 15.3 m. The horizontal speed plays no part in that, which is why a much flatter launch at the same speed reaches a lower peak. Integrating the vertical slowdown confirms the figure, since the height rises quadratically at first and stops rising exactly when the vertical speed reaches zero at the top of the arc.
questions.hint: The peak is where the vertical speed is zero, so use v squared equals 2 g h.

questions.topic: Range of a projectile over level ground
questions.learningObjective: compute the range of a projectile landing at its launch height
questions.stem: Fired over level ground at 20 m/s and 60 degrees above the horizontal, a ball travels until it lands again. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, what horizontal range in m does it cover?
questions.explanation: The range is the horizontal speed times the flight time, and the flight time is 3.53 s from the earlier calculation, so the range is 10 x 3.53 = 35.35 m. Getting there through the closed-form range rule, the horizontal component squared times the sine of twice the angle over g, gives the same number, which is the check that the two routes are consistent. The launch speed alone does not fix the range, since the angle decides how much of that speed goes into height rather than distance.
questions.hint: Multiply the horizontal speed by the time of flight, which comes from the vertical motion.

questions.topic: Velocity at the top of a projectile arc
questions.learningObjective: describe the velocity of a projectile at its highest point
questions.stem: A projectile is at the highest point of its flight. What are its velocity and acceleration at that instant?

options.text: Horizontal velocity only, with zero acceleration at the turning point
options.misconception: mistakes a zero vertical component for a zero weight

options.text: Downward velocity only, since the fall has already begun by the top
options.misconception: assumes the fall has started before the vertical velocity reverses

options.text: Horizontal velocity only, with a downward acceleration of g
Zero velocity, because everything stops at the top of a trajectory
options.misconception: confuses a zero vertical component with a zero velocity

questions.explanation: The vertical velocity is zero at the top, but the horizontal velocity never changed during the flight, so the projectile is still moving sideways. The acceleration is unchanged too: gravity still acts at full strength, and it is that continuing downward acceleration that turns the zero vertical velocity into a downward one immediately afterwards. Calling the top a moment of rest confuses a single component with the whole velocity, which is the standard way this question is misread.
questions.hint: Separate the two components and ask separately what has happened to each.

questions.topic: Drop time from a stated height
questions.learningObjective: find the fall time for a body dropped from rest
questions.stem: Released with no horizontal velocity from a height of 45 m above the ground, a ball falls straight down. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, how long in seconds does it take to reach the ground?
questions.explanation: Dropped from rest, the fall is a pure vertical launch, so the height is one half g t squared and 45 = 0.5 x 9.8 x t squared gives t as the root of 2 x 45 over 9.8, which is 3.03 s. This is the same computation as the time of flight of a projectile launched vertically at zero speed, so the two cases share one formula. The answer must be positive, and the fact that it does not depend on the ball's mass is the point of the free-fall result.
questions.hint: From rest the fall distance is one half g t squared, so solve for t.

questions.topic: Range at the 45 degree launch
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the range at the 45 degree launch angle
questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 45 degrees above the horizontal over level ground. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, what range in m does it achieve?
questions.explanation: At 45 degrees the two launch components are equal, each being 20 over the root of 2, so the range collapses to the launch speed squared over g, which is 400 over 9.8, or 40.82 m. The simplification is a coincidence of this angle: the cosine of 45 is the sine of 45 and the sine of twice 45 is one, so both awkward factors cancel. This is the range-maximising angle over level ground for a fixed speed, which is why the answer sets a ceiling that no other angle at 20 m/s can beat.
questions.hint: At 45 degrees the two components are equal and the range rule simplifies to v squared over g.

questions.topic: Equal ranges at complementary angles
questions.learningObjective: explain why complementary launch angles give the same range
questions.stem: Two launches of the same speed, one at 30 degrees and one at 60 degrees above the horizontal, are compared over level ground. What is the relationship between their ranges?

options.text: Neither can be compared without knowing the mass of the projectile
options.misconception: believes the mass changes a trajectory

options.text: The ranges are equal, because the two angles are complementary
The 60 degree launch goes further, since it spends longer in the air
options.misconception: weighs flight time against horizontal speed and picks the wrong one

options.text: The 30 degree launch goes further, since it keeps more of its speed forward
options.misconception: ignores the flight time gained by the steeper launch

questions.explanation: The range depends on the launch angle through the sine of twice that angle, and 30 and 60 degrees are complementary, so their doubles are 60 and 120 degrees. The sine of 60 degrees and the sine of 120 degrees are both 0.866, which is the same figure the cosine of 30 degrees gives, so the two angles enter the range rule identically. Working each launch out confirms it, giving 35.35 m for the flatter one and 35.35 m for the steeper, a difference of -7.1e-15 m, and either angle beats 45 degrees by exactly the same margin.
questions.hint: The range rule involves the sine of twice the launch angle, and the two doubles here are complementary too.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Centripetal acceleration from speed and radius
questions.learningObjective: compute a centripetal acceleration from a speed and a radius
questions.stem: Travelling at a constant 10 m/s around a circle of radius 5.0 m, a body must continually change the direction of its velocity. What centripetal acceleration in m/s^2 does it experience?
questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration is the square of the speed over the radius, so 10 squared over 5.0 gives 20 m/s^2. Reaching it another way, the angular speed is 10 over 5.0, which is 2.0 rad/s, and the product of that angular speed squared with the radius is the same 20 m/s^2. The speed is constant but the velocity is not, and this acceleration is what continually bends the velocity's direction; a body moving in a straight line at constant speed has none of it.
questions.hint: Divide the square of the speed by the radius, or use omega squared times r.

Working from the angular speed instead gives the same figure, since 2.0 rad/s squared times the 5.0 m radius is 20 m/s^2, and multiplying that by the mass is the same calculation in different notation. The force has no tangential component here because the speed is constant, so it acts purely to bend the path.
questions.hint: Multiply the centripetal acceleration by the mass to get the force.

The acceleration is never along the motion, since a tangential acceleration would change the speed, and it is never outward, because an outward force would bend the path the wrong way.

questions.topic: Normal force direction on a bank
questions.learningObjective: explain what the normal force does on a banked curve

options.misconception: credits the engine with a sideways force it cannot supply

options.text: The banked surface is curved, so gravity alone curves the car's path
options.misconception: believes gravity curves a path by itself, ignoring the surface

options.text: The car is steered into the turn, so the tyres supply the sideways force
options.misconception: believes steering removes the need for a sideways force

options.text: The tilted surface's normal force has a horizontal component pointing inward

questions.explanation: On a banked road the surface normal is tilted away from the vertical, so the normal force has a horizontal component directed toward the centre of the curve, and that component is exactly the centripetal force. The vertical component of the normal balances the weight in the vertical direction, so neither friction nor a sideways push is needed. Tilting the road therefore supplies the inward force geometrically, which is why the design works and why a level road of the same radius would demand a large friction force at speed.

questions.stem: A road is banked at 20 degrees on a curve of radius 50 m. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, what speed in m/s allows a car to take the curve with no friction at all?
questions.explanation: With no friction the horizontal part of the normal force must both balance the sideways need, m v squared over r, and follow from the vertical balance, where the normal is m g over the cosine of the bank angle. Dividing the two gives v squared equal to g r times the tangent of the bank angle, so the speed is the root of 9.8 x 50 x tan 20, which is 13.4 m/s. The radius enters linearly and the bank angle only through its tangent, so doubling the radius raises the speed by the root of two rather than doubling it.

Reversing the division, dividing the radius by the tangential speed, inverts the relation and produces a figure with the dimensions of a length rather than a rate. The radian is dimensionless in SI, so this angular speed carries its meaning through the ratio alone.

Getting there via the angular speed gives the same number, since 2 pi over 4.0 is the angular speed and dividing the tangential speed by it is the same ratio rearranged. options.misconception: forgets that the speed is squared in the centripetal relation

options.text: It halves, because a faster car needs less inward force to stay on the bend
options.misconception: believes a faster car needs a smaller inward force

options.text: It is unchanged, since the radius alone fixes the shape of the path
options.misconception: believes the radius alone fixes the required force

options.text: It quadruples, because the force depends on the square of the speed

questions.explanation: The centripetal force is m v squared over r, so with the mass and radius held fixed it rises as the square of the speed and quadrupling the speed quadruples the force. This is why motorway curves are built with much larger radii than junction roundabouts: the speed is higher, so the same radius would demand an unmanageable grip force. The radius enters only to the first power, so doubling the radius for the same speed would halve the demand, which is the other design lever.
questions.hint: Look at how the speed appears in the centripetal relation.

questions.explanation: The relative velocity is a componentwise difference, so subtracting the first car's velocity gives -15 m/s east and 10 m/s north, and the magnitude is the root of 225 plus 100, which is 18.03 m/s. It is not the difference of the two speeds, because the two motions point along different axes and a scalar subtraction would discard the geometry entirely. The two cars approach each other faster than either is travelling, which is why a pedestrian waiting to cross sees a closing rate that needs a square root to compute.

Writing the direction cosine as 0.6 gives the same figure, and the 3-4-5 triangle is the standard example because its cosine and sine are exact fractions. A direction cosine is a projection, so the two components together reconstruct the original length through Pythagoras rather than by addition.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: A position log misread as a velocity log
questions.learningObjective: identify the misreading behind a mislabelled table
questions.stem: A table labelled 'velocity against time' lists the values 0, 12, 48 and 108 m/s at 0, 1, 2 and 3 s. Treating it as a velocity record, what constant acceleration in m/s^2 does the first two entries imply?

options.text: 24 m/s^2, since the speed rises by twice that in the first two seconds
options.misconception: doubles the first-second change to get the second-second one

options.text: 0 m/s^2, since the entries are equally spaced in time rather than speed
options.misconception: confuses equal time intervals with equal velocity increments

options.text: 108 m/s^2, since the speed itself is the acceleration at the start
options.misconception: reads the velocity itself as though it were an acceleration

options.text: 12 m/s^2, since the speed rises by 12 m/s in the first second

questions.explanation: An acceleration is the change in velocity over the elapsed time, and the first second takes the velocity from 0 to 12 m/s, so the implied acceleration is 12 m/s^2. The later entries give a different figure, since 12 to 48 in one second is 36 m/s^2 and 48 to 108 is 60 m/s^2, so the label cannot be describing uniform acceleration at all and the table is internally inconsistent. That rising sequence of increments is the signature of a position record for a body speeding up, where the position differences are 12, 36 and 60 m rather than a constant velocity step.
questions.hint: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time, so use only the first second.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Resolving acceleration into components
questions.learningObjective: explain why an acceleration can be resolved into components
questions.stem: A car's velocity changes from due east to due north over a short time, so it has turned a right angle at a steady rate. What is true of its acceleration during that turn?

options.text: It is zero, because the speed of the car is unchanged through the turn
options.misconception: confuses a change in direction with a change in speed

options.text: It points away from the centre, since a change in direction pushes outward
options.misconception: confuses a centripetal acceleration with a centrifugal one

options.text: It has a component toward the turn's centre and none along the motion
It points along the direction of the new velocity, since that is where it goes
options.misconception: aligns the acceleration with the new direction of travel

questions.explanation: A change of direction at constant speed means the acceleration is entirely centripetal, pointing at the centre of the turn with no component along the direction of travel. Had the speed also changed, there would additionally be a tangential component along the motion, and the total acceleration would be the vector sum of the two. Equal speeds through the turn rule out the tangential part, and nothing pushes the car outward, so the last option inverts the physics.
questions.hint: Split the acceleration into a part along the motion and a part across it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Adding a current to a boat's own velocity
questions.learningObjective: combine a boat's velocity through the water with the current
questions.stem: A boat rows at 3.0 m/s across a river while the current carries it downstream at 4.0 m/s. What is the boat's speed relative to the bank in m/s?
questions.explanation: The boat's velocity through the water and the current's velocity are perpendicular, and velocities add, so the ground speed is the root of 9 plus 16, which is 5 m/s. The result must exceed the larger of the two, 4.0 m/s, and it does, which is the quick size check on the figure. Adding the two speeds to 7.0 m/s would describe a boat moving diagonally at a speed it cannot have, because the two contributions point along different axes.
questions.hint: Add the two velocities as perpendicular vectors, then take the magnitude.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: What a constant-velocity frame cannot detect
questions.learningObjective: explain what uniform motion cannot reveal about a frame
questions.stem: Inside a railway carriage moving at a steady 30 m/s, a ball rolls across the floor at 5 m/s toward the front. What speed does the ball have according to an observer on the ground beside the track?

options.text: 35 m/s, the sum of the carriage's speed and the ball's
25 m/s, the difference between the carriage's speed and the ball's
options.misconception: subtracts the two velocities as though they pointed opposite ways

options.text: 5 m/s, since the carriage's motion cannot change what the ball does
options.misconception: believes a frame's own motion makes no difference to any measurement inside it

options.text: 30 m/s, since the ball is carried along with the carriage
options.misconception: believes the ball's velocity relative to the ground equals the carriage's

questions.explanation: Velocities add when both point the same way, and the ball moves toward the front of a carriage that itself moves forward, so the ground observer adds 30 m/s to 5 m/s and finds 35 m/s. Subtracting them to get 25 m/s would be right only if the ball rolled toward the rear, and that is the classic test of whether the sign convention has been handled properly. The carriage's motion does change what a ground observer measures, even though it does not change anything about the motion seen from inside.
questions.hint: Both velocities point the same way, so ask whether they add or subtract.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: A launch that falls short of its target
questions.learningObjective: compare a range achieved with a range required
questions.stem: A target is 41 m away and a launcher fires at 45 degrees over level ground. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, what launch speed in m/s is needed, and how much range does a 19 m/s launch fall short by?
questions.explanation: At 45 degrees the range rule collapses to the speed squared over g, so the needed speed is the root of 41 x 9.8, which is the root of 401.8, and a 19 m/s launch instead reaches 36.8 m. The shortfall is the difference of the two, which is -3.98 m, negative because the achieved range is the smaller of the pair. Because the range goes as the square of the speed, a shortfall of a few metres in a range of about 40 m needs only a small speed shortfall, which is why the arithmetic here is less forgiving than it looks.
questions.hint: At 45 degrees the range is the speed squared over g, so find both speeds' ranges and subtract.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Components of a projectile's position at a time
questions.learningObjective: compute both position components of a projectile at a time
questions.stem: A projectile leaves the ground with components 8.0 m/s horizontal and 10 m/s vertical. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, what is its vertical position in m at t = 3.0 s, measured upward from the launch point?
questions.explanation: The vertical position is the vertical component times the time less half g t squared, so 10 x 3.0 minus 0.5 x 9.8 x 9 gives -14.1 m, which is negative because the projectile has already dropped below the level it was launched from. The horizontal position at the same instant is 24 m, so the projectile is well downrange and underground, which is what a vertical component of 10 m/s cannot sustain for 3 s. The negative sign is the useful signal here: a projectile launched at 10 m/s upward peaks after about 1.0 s and is back at its launch level after about 2.0 s.
questions.hint: Use the vertical component only, and expect a negative answer if 3 s is long after the apex.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Spotting an impossible velocity record
questions.learningObjective: detect a physically impossible entry in a motion log
questions.stem: A log lists a vehicle's positions at one-second intervals as 0 m, 20 m, 60 m, 120 m and 200 m, and the header claims constant speed. What is wrong with the header?

options.text: The header is correct, since the position differences are all different
options.misconception: mistakes differing distances for evidence of constant speed

options.text: The speed rises each second, so the motion is accelerating, not uniform
The positions are impossible, since a vehicle cannot travel 200 m in 4 s
options.misconception: believes a speed of 50 m/s is physically impossible for a vehicle

options.text: The positions are uniform in time, so the speed is in fact constant
options.misconception: confuses equal time intervals with equal distance intervals

questions.explanation: The distance covered in each second is 20 m, then 40 m, then 60 m, then 80 m, so the speed rises in equal steps from 20 m/s to 80 m/s and the motion is uniformly accelerated rather than uniform. Nothing here is physically impossible, since 200 m in 4 s is an average of 50 m/s, well within what a road vehicle can do. A constant-speed header would need equal position differences at equal time intervals, and these are the opposite of that.
questions.hint: Compute the distance covered in each one-second interval and compare the four values.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a frame of reference must be stated
questions.learningObjective: explain why a frame of reference must be stated with a velocity
questions.stem: A physics text says 'the plane's speed is 250 m/s' without saying relative to what, and a student asks why the omission matters. Explain why the frame of reference has to be named.

answer.exemplar: A speed is only ever a speed relative to something, and the plane's own motion is small compared with the rotation of the Earth, so quoting 250 m/s without a frame leaves the number ambiguous between the air, the ground and the Earth's centre. Relative to the air the figure would be the airspeed, relative to the ground the ground speed, and the two differ by the wind, which can be a large fraction of the difference. Relative to the Earth's centre the plane is also being carried round by the Earth's rotation at several hundred metres per second, so the choice of frame changes the number far more than any aerodynamic detail. A velocity is a difference between two positions measured in the same frame, so it is meaningless without one, and this is why flight planning quotes both the ground speed and the heading while a navigator corrects for the wind separately.

questions.explanation: A full answer should say that a velocity is a difference between two positions measured in the same frame, so it has no meaning without one, and then illustrate how the choice of frame changes the figure rather than just asserting it. Naming the ground, the air and the Earth's centre as three frames that would all give different numbers for the same flight shows the point concretely, and mentioning that a pilot must plan a flight by ground speed while the engines read airspeed gives it a practical consequence. The stronger answers also note that a uniform change of frame shifts every velocity by the frame's own velocity, which is the Galilean result the numerical items in this unit use.
questions.hint: Ask what a velocity is a difference of, and which two positions must be measured in the same frame.
